fatal_errors: The hypothesis replaces immersed reciprocating tribo-corrosion in deionized water at 25–100 °C with static molten-salt corrosion at 450–650 °C.

Neither the proposed intervention nor the falsification experiment includes sliding contact, load, frequency, counter-body, friction, wear-volume measurement, or sliding-induced depassivation, so they cannot establish tribo-corrosion resistance.
The cited evidence supports molten-salt corrosion rates, not the asserted performance under tribo-corrosion.

The proposed selective-dissolution and noble-element enrichment mechanism does not reconstruct the target mechanism involving passive-film repair, tribo-layer stability, abrasion, and temperature-dependent wear transitions.
explanation: The response correctly identifies AlCoCrFeNi2.1 and DS2205 as the material and comparator, and its numerical molten-salt corrosion claims are traceable to the cited paper. However, it appears to reconstruct a different study. The target used an L12/B2 lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy after rapid thermal-shock cycles and alumina-ball reciprocating tribo-corrosion in deionized water. Its key findings were phase retention, approximately order-of-magnitude lower wear, lower friction, more stable passivation, and minimum degradation near 50 °C. The generated hypothesis instead addresses non-tribological molten-salt corrosion at 450 and 650 °C and reports corrosion rates that do not predict the target wear or friction outcomes. Its experiment is capable of distinguishing molten-salt corrosion behavior but cannot test the stated tribo-corrosion claim, making the evidence-to-claim transfer invalid.
